body.en: Equity shares represent ownership: holders get dividends only from profits, have voting rights and bear the highest risk, but the company has no fixed burden. Preference shares get a fixed rate of dividend and repayment of capital before equity holders, usually without voting rights. Retained profits (ploughing back) are profits kept in the business: a cheap, internal source with no dilution of control. Debentures and bonds are borrowed capital carrying a fixed rate of interest, payable even in a loss, and usually secured on assets. Public deposits are taken directly from the public for 6 months to 3 years. Term loans come from banks and financial institutions.

points.en: Retained profits: internal, no cost of issue
Debentures and bonds: fixed interest, creditors

title.en: Short-term sources and choosing a source

body.en: Working capital is met by *short-term sources*. Trade credit is credit given by suppliers on purchases. Discounting of bills of exchange gets cash from a bank before a bill's due date. Factoring is selling book debts to a factor, who collects them and pays most of the value at once. Bank overdrafts and cash credit are also used. A firm chooses a source by cost, risk, the period of need, control, flexibility and the state of the market. Using fixed-cost debt when the return on investment exceeds the interest rate raises the return to shareholders: this is trading on equity.

problem.en: A company needs ₹50 crore and expects a return of 8% on it. It can borrow at 12%. Should it raise 60% by debentures? Compare EPS with all-equity finance (shares of ₹10, tax ignored).

steps.en: With 60% debt: interest = 12% of 30 = ₹3.6 crore; profit = ₹0.4 crore; shares = 2 crore; EPS = ₹0.20.
ROI (8%) is below the interest rate (12%), so debt lowers EPS.

answer.en: No: EPS falls from ₹0.80 to ₹0.20, because the return is below the cost of debt.

narration.en: Let us work this out step by step. A company needs ₹50 crore and expects a return of 8% on it. It can borrow at 12%. Should it raise 60% by debentures? Compare EPS with all-equity finance (shares of ₹10, tax ignored).

say.en: Let us work this out step by step. A company needs 50 rupees crore and expects a return of 8 percent on it. It can borrow at 12 percent. Should it raise 60 percent by debentures? Compare EPS with all-equity finance (shares of 10, rupees tax ignored).
EBIT equals 8 percent of 50 equals 4 rupees crore.
All equity: 5 crore shares; EPS equals 4 over 5 equals 0.80 rupees.
With 60 percent debt: interest equals 12 percent of 30 equals 3.6 rupees crore; profit equals 0.4 rupees crore; shares equals 2 crore; EPS equals 0.20 rupees.
ROI 8 percent is below the interest rate 12 percent, so debt lowers EPS.
So the answer is No: EPS falls from 0.80 rupees to 0.20 rupees, because the return is below the cost of debt.
